lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Generating Electricity from Thermal and Nuclear Power Stations

pages.body:
Most of the electricity used in Ghana is made in power stations. Some are built beside rivers and use falling water. Others burn fuel such as natural gas or oil.

- What do you think a power station must do to produce electricity?
- Have you heard of nuclear power? What do you think is different about it?

Electricity does not occur freely in a form we can use, so it must be generated. In this lesson we study the idea behind electricity generation and then examine two kinds of power station, thermal and nuclear.

Before we look at the two types of power station, we need the one idea they share.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The basic idea of generating electricity

pages.title: The basic idea of generating electricity
pages.body:
Nearly all large power stations use a generator. A generator makes electricity when a coil of wire and a magnet move relative to each other. A shaft turns the generator, and this shaft is turned by a machine called a turbine. A turbine is a wheel with blades that spins when a fast moving fluid such as steam, water or wind pushes against it. Power stations differ mainly in how they supply the energy that turns the turbine.

We begin with thermal power stations, which use heat from burning fuel.

pages.title: Thermal electricity
pages.body: In a thermal power station a fuel is burned to release heat. The fuel may be natural gas, crude oil, diesel or coal. The heat boils water in a boiler to make steam at high pressure. The steam is directed onto the blades of a turbine and makes it spin. The turbine turns the generator, which produces electricity. After passing through the turbine, the steam is cooled in a condenser and changed back to water to be used again. Some gas fuelled stations burn the gas to turn a turbine directly, and use the hot exhaust to make steam as well.

Ghana has thermal power stations at places such as Aboadze near Takoradi and at Tema. The energy changes in a thermal station are chemical energy in the fuel to heat energy to kinetic energy of the steam and turbine, and finally to electrical energy.

Next we study nuclear power stations, which also make steam but get their heat in a different way.

## Nuclear electricity

In a nuclear power station the heat comes from nuclear fission, not from burning. Fission is the splitting of the nucleus of a heavy atom such as uranium into smaller parts. When a nucleus splits it releases a very large amount of heat and also releases neutrons, which split other nuclei. This repeating process is called a chain reaction. The reaction takes place in a reactor, where control rods absorb extra neutrons to keep the rate of reaction safe. The heat is used to make steam, and from that point the process is the same as in a thermal station. The steam turns the turbine, the turbine turns the generator and electricity is produced.

A very small amount of uranium can release as much heat as a very large amount of coal. Ghana has a small nuclear research reactor at the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission at Kwabenya, which is used for research and training and not to supply electricity. Ghana has also been studying whether to build a nuclear power station in the future.

[[pic: Block diagram of a thermal power station showing fuel, boiler, steam, turbine, generator and condenser. Beside it, a block diagram of a nuclear power station with reactor, control rods, steam, turbine and generator.]]

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Generating Electricity from Thermal and Nuclear Power Stations (part 4)

pages.body:
| **Feature** | **Thermal power station** | **Nuclear power station** |
|---|---|---|
| Source of heat | Burning a fuel such as gas, oil or coal | Nuclear fission of uranium |
| Fuel used | Natural gas, crude oil, diesel or coal | Uranium |
| Main waste | Carbon dioxide and other gases, and ash with some fuels | Radioactive waste |
| How steam turns the turbine | The same in both stations | The same in both stations |

> **Did you know?** Both thermal and nuclear power stations are called heat engines. They change heat energy into electrical energy, but no heat engine can change all the heat into electricity. A large part of the heat is lost to the surroundings.

pages.body:
A large power station is built near your community. Some people welcome it because it will bring electricity. Others are worried about smoke, noise and what may happen to the sea or river nearby.

- What possible harm to the environment can you think of?
- How could this harm be reduced?

No source of electricity is free of effects on the environment. In this lesson we study the negative effects of thermal and nuclear power generation, how they can be reduced and how to prepare for a class debate.

We start with thermal power stations, because they burn fuel.

pages.title: Effects of thermal power stations
pages.body:
- Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the atmosphere and contributes to global warming and climate change.
- Burning fuel also releases sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. These gases dissolve in rainwater to form acid rain, which harms plants, soil, buildings and water life.
- Smoke, soot and fine particles from burning, especially from coal and oil, cause breathing problems.
- Water used to cool the plant is returned to the sea or river warm. This thermal pollution can reduce the oxygen in the water and harm fish and other aquatic life.
- Drilling, mining and transporting fuel can damage land and cause oil spills.

Now we turn to the effects of nuclear power stations, which are very different.

pages.title: Effects of nuclear power stations
pages.body:
- A nuclear station releases almost no carbon dioxide while it operates, so it adds very little to global warming. It still has other serious effects.
- Used fuel and other waste are radioactive. Radioactive waste can harm living things and stays dangerous for a very long time, sometimes for thousands of years, so it must be stored safely.
- An accident can release radioactive material into the air, soil and water. The accidents at Chernobyl in Ukraine in 1986 and at Fukushima in Japan in 2011 forced thousands of people to leave their homes.
- Cooling water returned to rivers or the sea is warmer and can cause thermal pollution, just as in thermal stations.
- Mining and processing uranium can damage the environment.

| **Effect** | **Thermal station** | **Nuclear station** |
|---|---|---|
| Greenhouse gas | Large amounts of carbon dioxide | Almost none during operation |
| Air pollution | Sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particles | Very little in normal operation |
| Waste | Gases, and ash with some fuels | Radioactive waste that needs long term safe storage |
| Risk of serious accident | Fires, explosions and oil spills | Release of radioactive material |
| Water | Warm cooling water | Warm cooling water |

We now consider practical ways to reduce the damage.

pages.title: Reducing the harmful effects
pages.body:
- Use cleaner fuels such as natural gas in place of coal or oil, and fit filters that trap smoke and harmful gases.
- Build efficient stations that waste less heat, so less fuel is burned for the same electricity.
- Store radioactive waste in strong sealed containers in safe places that are far from water sources and homes.
- Train workers well, inspect plants regularly and prepare emergency plans.
- Cool the water before releasing it, or release it far from sensitive habitats.
- Add renewable sources such as hydro, solar and wind to the supply, and use electricity wisely at home and in school.
- Plant trees, which absorb some of the carbon dioxide.
Finally we prepare for a class debate on the motion that thermal and nuclear power stations do more harm than good.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Preparing for the debate and the poster

pages.title: Preparing for the debate and the poster
pages.body:
1. Divide the class into a team that supports the motion, a team that opposes it and a panel of judges.
2. Each team searches for facts about thermal and nuclear electricity, noting where each fact came from.
3. Each speaker presents one point supported by a fact. Teams then reply to the other side.
4. The judges award marks for clear points, use of facts and respect for others.
5. Together, the class designs a poster or leaflet that shows the main effects and ways to reduce them.

[[pic: Sample poster layout with the title Making Electricity Safely, a drawing of a power station with smoke, a column of harmful effects and a column of ways to reduce them.]]

questions.q: Name three harmful effects of thermal power stations on the environment.
Name two harmful effects of nuclear power stations on the environment.
Explain how thermal pollution can harm fish.
Suggest two ways in which the effects of thermal power stations can be reduced.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Electronic Components and the Resistor Colour Code

pages.body:
Open the back of a spoilt radio or a mobile phone charger, with an adult present and the battery removed. You will see a green or brown board with many small parts joined by thin metal lines.

- What do you think each of the small parts is doing?
- Why do you think there are so many different shapes and colours?

Electronic devices such as radios, phones, calculators and televisions are built from small parts called electronic components. In this lesson we examine the main components, learn to read the colour code of a resistor and see how components are arranged in a circuit.

We begin by seeing how electronics differs from ordinary electrical wiring.

pages.title: What electronics is
pages.body:
Electronics is the branch of science and technology that controls the flow of small electric currents with components made mostly from materials called semiconductors. Electrical wiring in a house carries large currents to run heaters and lamps. Electronic circuits carry small currents to do things such as amplify sound, store information or switch a small light on and off.

Next we study each component, what it looks like and what it does.

pages.title: The main electronic components
pages.body:
- A resistor limits the amount of current in a circuit. It is a small cylinder with coloured bands. Its value is measured in ohms.
- A capacitor stores electric charge for a short time and releases it when needed. It has two conducting plates separated by an insulator. Its value is measured in farads, though most capacitors in small devices are rated in much smaller units.
- A diode allows current to flow in one direction only. It is made from a PN junction, which joins a P type semiconductor to an N type semiconductor.
- A light emitting diode, or LED, is a special diode that gives out light when current flows through it in the correct direction. It has two legs, and the longer leg is the positive leg, called the anode. The shorter leg is the negative leg, called the cathode.
- An inductor is a coil of wire that stores energy in a magnetic field when current flows through it and opposes sudden changes in current.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Electronic Components and the Resistor Colour Code (part 3)

pages.body:
LEDs come in several types. Small indicator LEDs, usually 3 millimetres or 5 millimetres wide, are used as power lights on radios and chargers. They are made in red, green, yellow, blue and white. RGB LEDs contain red, green and blue lights in one case and can show many colours. High power LEDs are used in torches, street lamps and room lighting. Flat surface mount LEDs are used on the circuit boards of phones and televisions.

[[pic: Row of drawings of a resistor, a capacitor, a diode, an LED and an inductor next to their circuit symbols. Label the anode and cathode on the diode and the LED.]]

A resistor is too small to print its value in numbers, so bands of colour are used.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Reading the colour code of a resistor

pages.title: Reading the colour code of a resistor
pages.body:
Hold the resistor so that the gold or silver band is on the right. Read the bands from the left. The first two bands give the first two digits. The third band tells how many zeros follow, which is the multiplier. The last band shows how accurate the value is, called the tolerance.

| **Colour** | **Digit** | **Colour** | **Digit** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Black | 0 | Green | 5 |
| Brown | 1 | Blue | 6 |
| Red | 2 | Violet | 7 |
| Orange | 3 | Grey | 8 |
| Yellow | 4 | White | 9 |

A gold fourth band means a tolerance of 5 percent and a silver fourth band means 10 percent. Here are two worked examples.

- Brown, black, red, gold. The first two digits are 1 and 0. The multiplier is red, which means two zeros, so the value is 1000 ohms, or 1 kilohm, with a tolerance of 5 percent.
- Yellow, violet, orange, gold. The first two digits are 4 and 7. The multiplier is orange, which means three zeros, so the value is 47 000 ohms, or 47 kilohms, with a tolerance of 5 percent.

Finally we see how these components are connected to make a working circuit.

pages.title: Arranging components in a circuit
pages.body: An electronic circuit is a closed path along which current flows through components that are joined by conducting wires or by metal tracks on a circuit board. A simple circuit has a source of electrical energy such as a battery, a switch to control the current, a resistor to limit the current and an LED to show that current is flowing. The components are joined in series in a loop, so the same current passes through each one. It is important to connect the LED the right way round because it will only light when its anode is joined towards the positive side of the battery.

[[pic: Circuit diagram showing a battery, a switch, a resistor and an LED connected in series in a loop with the anode of the LED facing the positive terminal of the battery.]]

> **Did you know?** A modern mobile phone contains billions of tiny electronic switches made from semiconductors, packed into chips smaller than a fingernail.

questions.q: State the job of a resistor and of a capacitor in an electronic circuit.
Name the legs of an LED and state how to recognise each one.
A resistor has the colour bands red, red, brown, gold. Work out its value.
Explain why an LED connected the wrong way round does not light.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Assembling a Simple Circuit with a PN Junction Diode and an LED

pages.body:
Think about a torch. When you slide the switch, the bulb lights at once. When you slide it back, the bulb goes out.

- What do you think is happening inside the torch when the switch is on and when it is off?
- What do you think would happen if you put the batteries in the wrong way round?

In this lesson we examine the PN junction in a diode, build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and an LED, and explain what happens when the switch is opened and closed. We also learn how to dismantle spoilt gadgets safely to name their parts.

We begin with the structure of a diode, which is the heart of an LED.

pages.title: The PN junction diode
pages.body: A diode is made by joining two types of semiconductor material. The P region has an excess of positive charge carriers, and the N region has an excess of negative charge carriers, which are electrons. The place where they meet is called the PN junction. When the positive terminal of a battery is connected to the P side and the negative terminal to the N side, current flows through the diode. This is called forward connection. When the connections are reversed, the diode blocks the current. This one way property is why a diode is often compared to a valve.

[[pic: Diagram of a PN junction diode showing the P region, the N region and the junction between them. Beside it, the diode symbol with the anode on the P side and the cathode on the N side with a bar.]]

Now we use the diode, in the form of an LED, to build a simple working circuit.

pages.title: Building the circuit
pages.body:
1. Collect two dry cells of 1.5 volts each, a switch, an LED, a resistor of about 100 to 220 ohms, a holder for the cells and connecting wires.
2. Place the two cells in series in the holder, positive to negative, to give a total of 3 volts.
3. Connect the positive terminal of the battery to one side of the switch.
4. Connect the other side of the switch to the resistor, and the resistor to the long leg of the LED, which is the anode.
5. Connect the short leg of the LED, the cathode, back to the negative terminal of the battery.
6. Check every connection with your teacher before closing the switch.

The resistor is included to protect the LED. A 3 volt battery connected directly to an LED can pass too much current and damage it, so a resistor is added in series to limit the current.

Next we explain how the switch controls the circuit.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: What happens when the switch is closed and opened

pages.title: What happens when the switch is closed and opened
pages.body:
When the switch is closed, the circuit forms a complete loop, so current flows from the battery through the switch, the resistor and the LED and back to the battery. The LED lights. When the switch is opened, there is a gap in the loop, and the current stops flowing, so the LED goes out. If the LED is connected the wrong way round, the diode blocks the current and the LED will not light even when the switch is closed.

Finally we practise examining the parts inside real gadgets.

pages.title: Dismantling and assembling spoilt gadgets
pages.body:
Spoilt gadgets such as radios, remote controls, electronic watches and mobile phones can be opened to show the components inside. Only do this with your teacher present.

- Remove the batteries and unplug the gadget from the mains before opening it.
- Do not open the back of a television set or computer monitor because some parts can store a dangerous charge even when switched off.
- Use a small screwdriver and keep the screws in a dish so that none is lost.
- Name and sketch each part you can see, such as the circuit board, the speaker, the battery holder, resistors, capacitors, diodes, LEDs and switches.
- Try to put the gadget back together in the correct order.

Explain why a resistor is placed in series with the LED.
State two safety rules to follow when dismantling a spoilt radio.

pages.body:
A school electronics club builds a circuit with a battery, a resistor and an LED. When they replace the resistor with a larger one, the LED becomes dim.

- Why do you think the LED became dim?
- What do you think would happen if there were no resistor at all?

No component works alone in a circuit. In this lesson we describe what each of four important components does and how they depend on each other, and we explain how adding each of them changes the brightness of an LED.

We start with the LED, the part of the circuit that shows what is happening.

pages.title: The LED
pages.body:
The LED is a diode that gives out light when current flows through it in the forward direction. It uses very little power and lasts for a long time, so it is widely used in torches, indicators on appliances and room lighting. An LED is easily damaged by too much current, so it must always be used with a part that limits the current.

Next we study the part that protects the LED.

pages.title: The resistor
pages.body:
A resistor opposes the flow of current and so limits it. The larger the resistance, the smaller the current for the same battery. Current is found by dividing voltage by resistance. In our circuit with a 3 volt battery and a 100 ohm resistor, the LED takes up about 2 volts, so about 1 volt is left across the resistor. The current is about 1 divided by 100, which is 0.01 ampere, or 10 milliamperes. This is a safe current for a small LED.

Now we study the one way valve of the circuit.

pages.title: The diode
pages.body:
A diode lets current pass in one direction only. In a circuit it can protect other parts from damage if the battery is connected the wrong way round, because it blocks the reversed current. When current does pass through a silicon diode in the forward direction, about 0.7 volts is used up by the diode.

Finally we study the coil that reacts to changes in current.

pages.title: The inductor
pages.body:
An inductor is a coil of wire. When current passes through it a magnetic field forms around it and energy is stored in that field. The inductor opposes any sudden change in current. When the switch is closed the current rises gradually rather than instantly, and when the switch is opened the inductor tries to keep the current flowing for a very short time. In a steady direct current circuit an inductor has little effect once the current has settled, but in a circuit with changing current, such as in a radio, it has a large effect.

Here we use these ideas to predict what happens to an LED when components are added to the circuit.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How added components change the brightness of an LED

pages.title: How added components change the brightness of an LED
pages.body:
| **Change made to the circuit** | **Effect on the LED** | **Reason** |
|---|---|---|
| A larger resistor is added in series | Becomes dimmer | More resistance gives less current |
| A smaller resistor replaces a larger one | Becomes brighter | Less resistance gives more current, but too little resistance can damage the LED |
| A diode is added in series in the forward direction | Slightly dimmer | The diode uses up part of the voltage |
| A diode is added in series in the reverse direction | Goes out | The diode blocks the current |
| An inductor is added in series in a steady direct current circuit | Rises slowly at switch on and then looks almost the same | The inductor opposes sudden change but not steady current |
To end the lesson we see how the four components rely on one another.

pages.title: Interdependence of the components
pages.body:
- The LED depends on the resistor to limit the current so that it does not burn out.
- The resistor depends on the battery to supply a voltage so that current flows.
- The diode depends on correct connection of the battery. It protects the LED and other parts from reverse current.
- The inductor depends on a changing current in order to show its effect, and it protects other parts from sudden surges.
- If any one component fails or is connected wrongly, the whole circuit can stop working.

Explain why the components in a circuit are said to depend on one another.

pages.body:
- A generator, turned by a turbine, makes electricity. Power stations differ in how they supply the energy that turns the turbine.
- A thermal power station burns fuel to make steam. A nuclear power station gets its heat from nuclear fission, and both use steam to turn a turbine.
- Thermal stations release carbon dioxide and other pollutants. Nuclear stations produce radioactive waste and carry the risk of serious accidents.
- The harmful effects of electricity generation can be reduced by cleaner fuels, filters, safe waste storage, careful management, renewable sources and saving electricity.
- The main electronic components are the resistor, the capacitor, the diode, the LED and the inductor.
- The colour bands of a resistor give its value in ohms and its tolerance.
- A PN junction diode allows current in one direction only. An LED is a diode that gives out light.
- When a switch is closed, current flows and the LED lights. When it is opened the circuit is broken and the LED goes out.
- Adding a larger resistor makes an LED dimmer, a reversed diode puts it out and an inductor opposes sudden changes in current.
